Does kinematic gait quality improve with functional gait recovery? A
longitudinal pilot study on early post-stroke individuals
Sung Yul Shina
, Robert K. Leeb
, Patrick Spicerc
, James Sulzera,⇑
a
Department of Mechanical Engineering, University of Texas at Austin, USA
b
St. David’s Rehabilitation Hospital, St. David’s Medical Center, USA
c
Seton Brain and Spine Institute, Ascension, TX, USA
a r t i c l e i n f o
Article history:
Accepted 20 March 2020
Available online xxxx
Keywords:
Gait
Gait quality
Functional gait recovery
Stroke
Inertial measurement units
a b s t r a c t
Typical clinical gait outcomes mostly focus on function; only sparse information exists on gait quality, i.e.
symmetry or more natural gait patterns. It remains unclear whether functional gait recovery improves
with gait quality, or whether these are two independent processes. The objective of this observational
pilot study is to examine whether the gait quality improves with gait function (i.e. speed) over the course
of early recovery. Full lower body gait kinematics were measured longitudinally in a clinical environment
using wearable inertial measurement units. We recorded six individuals with subacute stroke (<1 month)
for a total of 56 physical therapy sessions over the initial recovery stage of 12 weeks. We examined rela-
tions between gait symmetry in spatiotemporal, limb and joint kinematic parameters compared to gait
function. We observed that overall gait symmetry improved with walking speed, but limb and joint kine-
matic parameters remained asymmetric at the maximum level of recovery (both p < 0.01). We also found
that limb kinematic parameters (R2
= 41.9%) of the impaired side was preferentially associated with func-
tional gait recovery over joint kinematics (R2
= 33.1%). These data suggest that our pilot cohort did not
achieve ‘‘true” gait recovery despite achieving typical measures of recovery in gait speed and spatiotem-
poral symmetry. These initial results illustrate the multifaceted nature of recovery and justify further
research on monitoring gait quality with a larger clinical study, providing insight for more effective train-
ing regimens.
Ó 2020 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved.
1. Introduction
Restoration of gait and motor recovery following neurological
injury such as stroke involves improvements both in functional
ability and quality of movements. However, typical clinical out-
comes for measuring gait are mostly focused on functional ability
such as gait speed (Tilson et al., 2010), timed-up-and-go
(Podsiadlo and Richardson, 1991), six minute walk (Enright,
2003), and others, whereas gait quality is ignored. Disturbances
in gait quality are associated with an increased risk of falls
(Weerdesteyn et al., 2008), greater energy expenditure (Finley
et al., 2013) and may lead to long-term problems such as learned
non-use or use-dependent plasticity and pain (Jones, 2017; Levin
et al., 2009). For instance, patients with asymmetric gait have
shown greater metabolic energy expenditure from 50% to 67%
more than that of body weight-matched healthy controls with
same walking speed (Woolley, 2001).
Parameters to measure gait quality can be broken down into
more than just spatiotemporal characteristics (i.e., step length or
step time). Spatiotemporal symmetry has been well charted in
post-stroke individuals (Balasubramanian et al., 2007; Patterson
et al., 2015, 2010). However, stroke survivors exhibit significant
asymmetry in joint kinematics with greater inter-individual
variability than spatiotemporal characteristics (Woolley, 2001).
Typical asymmetry in joint kinematics includes reduced hip
extension, knee flexion and ankle dorsi/plantarflexion, and knee
hyperextension on the impaired side (Kim and Eng, 2004; Perry
and Burnfield, 1992). While these studies have attempted to char-
acterize disturbances in joint kinematics after stroke, the majority
report instantaneous or short-term measurements on chronic
patients (Kim and Eng, 2004; Woolley, 2001). There is currently a
lack of information regarding how these joint kinematics change
over the course of recovery, especially the critical subacute phase
(<3 months).
Limb kinematics, used to describe end-effector (i.e. foot) motion
in task space, can be used to characterize locomotor function. For
instance, Chang et al. suggested that joint kinematics were

--- PAGE 2 ---
coordinated with greater variance to preferentially conserve and
stabilize the limb kinematics of walking after neuromuscular
injury of cats (Chang et al., 2009). It is reflective of the concept of
an uncontrolled manifold hypothesis, where control degrees-of-
freedom are reduced by allowing variability in uncontrolled vari-
ables (Scholz and Schöner, 1999). In humans, however, no evidence
exists to show how spatiotemporal characteristics, along with limb
or joint kinematics, change over the course of early recovery and
whether they correspond with gait function. Characterizing how
these gait parameters change over recovery can help determine
how to time interventions to maximize function.
The objective of this observational study is to examine changes
in gait quality in terms of spatiotemporal, limb and joint kinemat-
ics over the initial stage of recovery. The primary technical chal-
lenge of this endeavor is measuring kinematics in a clinical
environment longitudinally. We overcame this problem by using
portable, unobtrusive inertial motion capture to measure gait kine-
matics over the initial recovery stage of 12 weeks. Since asymme-
try in joint kinematics shows greater variability than
spatiotemporal characteristics (Woolley, 2001), we expected that
gait quality will remain asymmetric over the course of early recov-
ery, driven by joint kinematics. Secondly, we also expected that in
the impaired side, limb kinematic parameters will associate with
gait speed more than joint kinematics, suggesting an uncontrolled
manifold in the joint kinematics domain.
This preliminary study describes a novel characterization of dis-
turbances in gait quality during the early recovery process after
stroke. The information from this study details the importance of
gait quality, it helps delineate underlying kinematic mechanisms
of gait recovery, and provides insight for more effective therapy
regimens.
2. Methods
2.1. Participants
We recruited nine individuals with subacute stroke (<1 month)
to participate in this study approved by the University of Texas
Institutional Review Board and St. David’s Medical Center, Austin,
TX. Among nine patients, six individuals were longitudinally mon-
itored for a total of 56 physical therapy sessions consisting of gait-
related activity. Individuals ranged in age and impairment level
(see Table 1). Inclusion criteria of this study were: ischemic cere-
bral infarction based on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data,
hemiparesis, premorbidly independent, within two weeks follow-
ing injury or as soon as able to participate in gait training deter-
mined by the physical therapist. Exclusion criteria include
cerebellar damage, prior stroke, stroke-related pain syndromes,
or functionally relevant neuromuscular impairments. Participants
were allowed to use any assistive devices including a wheelchair,
body weight support, walker, cane or ankle foot orthosis (AFO)
during sessions if necessary (see Table 1). Prior to the first session,
the experimenter and therapist explained all the experimental pro-
cedures to each participant and obtained informed consent. We
began monitoring as soon as participants were capable of begin-
ning gait therapy, i.e., as soon as walk independently without ther-
apist’s full assistance. Three participants were excluded from the
dataset because two of them were not able to walk before dis-
charge and one discharged before the recording session. Three of
the participants included in this analysis completed less than the
full 12 recording sessions. One participant was discharged to a dif-
ferent hospital (P2), one lacked sufficient insurance coverage (P3),
and one was discharged to home therapy (P4).
2.2. Experimental setup and protocol
Our goal was to consecutively monitor gait kinematics during
physical therapy sessions. We targeted a maximum of 12 recording
sessions over the course of the first three months throughout the
inpatient to outpatient phases. Our recording session frequency
was greater in the earlier stages of recovery, i.e. two/week for three
weeks, one/week for four weeks, then one every other week. For
each session, we attached seven commercial inertial measurement
unit (IMU) motion sensors (XSens, Enschede, The Netherlands) on
the pelvis and bilaterally on thighs, shanks and feet using custom-
made elastic bands. The anthropometric measurements were esti-
mated by height of each subject and used as input of the IMU soft-
ware (Winter, 2009). IMUs measured three-dimensional
orientations of all lower body segments as well as joint angle tra-
jectories at a sampling rate of 60 Hz. Data was transmitted wire-
lessly to a commercial Latitude E5470 laptop (Dell Computers,
Round Rock, TX).
The total setup time took approximately 10–20 min. All setup
was performed immediately prior to the normally scheduled phys-
ical therapy sessions. After donning sensors, participants were
asked to maintain a straight standing position for five seconds to
calibrate the system as recommended by proprietary IMU manu-
facturer. Therapist assistance was provided for this calibration as
necessary. Following calibration, participants performed typical
1-hour training under the supervision of a physical therapist incor-
porating a number of tasks including overground and treadmill
walking. The experimenter used a cart to follow the participant
and therapist to maintain wireless communication of sensor sig-
nals (approximately 3–5 m away from the participant). After the
session, all sensors were removed from the participant.
2.3. Gait features and outcomes
On average, approximately 45.5% of the duration of the 1-hour
therapy session was dedicated to gait training. For each session, we
sampled normal, straight overground walking (between 5 and 80
strides depending on participant’s severity) at a comfortable speed
to extract gait quality measures. Custom software was written in

--- PAGE 3 ---
MATLAB (Mathworks, Inc. R2016a, Natick, MA) to calculate the
outcomes. The joint angle trajectories of the sampled gait portion
were truncated and normalized into 100% of gait cycle from heel
strike to heel strike of the left foot (Zeni Jr. et al., 2008). Fig. 1 illus-
trates an example of recorded gait kinematics data from a session
including bilateral joint angle trajectories of single gait cycle in
sagittal plane. Outcomes were extracted by imposing the gait kine-
matics data into a lower body kinematic model with the lower
limb lengths estimated by the anthropometric data based on
height of each individuals as described below (Winter, 2009).
Spatiotemporal parameters included step length (SL) and step
time (ST), defined as the linear distance between right and left feet,
and the duration of each step, respectively (Fig. 2, left). Limb kine-
matic parameters incorporated limb length (LL) (Chang et al.,
2009), leg extension angle (LEA) (Peterson et al., 2010), and foot
path area (FPA) (Banala et al., 2009) defined as the range of linear
distance between hip and foot, the angle between a line from hip to
the foot and vertical before toe-off, and area of foot pattern from
hip in sagittal plane during gait cycle, respectively (Fig. 2, middle).
Joint kinematic parameters were defined as the range of motion
(RoM) from selected joint variables, including all three rotations
of hip, knee flex/extension and ankle dorsi/plantarflexion (Fig. 2,
right). All parameters involved affected and unaffected sides,
enabling symmetry analysis.
We selected gait speed as the main outcome measure represen-
tative of functional gait recovery (Holleran et al., 2014; Hornby
et al., 2016). The number of strides for each session was varied (be-
tween 5 and 80 strides) due to different impairment levels within
and between subjects. In each session, the average gait speed was
calculated by dividing average stride distance by the average time
of gait cycles. A simple correlation analysis showed a strong
association between calculated gait speed and clinical outcome
measure, the six-minute walk test (r = 0.91).
2.4. Gait asymmetry measures
2.4.1. Overall gait asymmetry
Gait symmetry, and its inverse, asymmetry, are common mea-
sures of gait quality (Ramakrishnan et al., 2018; Viteckova et al.,
2018). In its simplest form, symmetry is represented by the ratio
of stance time on each limb or step length (Balasubramanian
et al., 2007). However, spatiotemporal asymmetry does not neces-
sarily equate with asymmetry in other domains such as kinemat-
ics. Here we combined all the aforementioned gait parameters
into one asymmetry measure by employing the combined gait
asymmetry metric (CGAM) (Ramakrishnan et al., 2018). The CGAM
combines different asymmetry parameters using the Mahalanobis
distance. Mahalanobis distance is a distance measure of a
multi-dimensional data point in a data distribution space (De
Maesschalck et al., 2000). Compared to Euclidean distance, the
Mahalanobis distance takes covariance of data into account to
standardize the scaling of distance measure in multi-dimensional
space. The CGAM uses the Mahalanobis distance from ideal sym-
metry (i.e., zero) to the asymmetry ratio obtained from gait param-
eters. For each session, the asymmetry ratio of ith
gait parameter
was calculated with the asymmetry ratio index given by

asymmetry of parameters from spatiotemporal, limb and joint kine-
matic domains was then evaluated with the Mahalanobis dis-
tance,Dm, given by

parameters (Ramakrishnan et al., 2018). As a basis for comparison,
we extracted the symmetric threshold based on the AR of our gait
database (Yun et al., 2014) obtained from 113 healthy individuals
walking at 3 km/h (Table 2). The symmetric threshold for CGAM
was then calculated by combining those symmetric threshold val-
ues of input gait parameters, and defined as ‘‘symmetric” walking
if the Mahalanobis distance,Dm, was less than the symmetric
threshold of CGAM.
2.4.2. Asymmetry of individual gait parameters
The asymmetry of individual parameters in spatiotemporal (SL,
ST), limb (LL, LEA, FPA) and joint kinematic (RoMs) domains was
then independently analyzed to explore the main contributor of
overall gait asymmetry. AR was used to evaluate asymmetry of
individual parameters. Note that with the absolute value in Eq.
(1), the asymmetry ratio only indicates whether each parameter
is asymmetric or not, without taking into account the direction
of which side is greater. Similar to overall asymmetry, an asymme-
try ratio less than the symmetric threshold value obtained from
Table 2 was considered ‘‘symmetric” walking for the individual
parameters.

2.4.3. Limb vs. joint kinematics
Each limb and joint kinematic parameter was transformed into
a common space (i.e., domain) using the Mahalanobis distance
metric, which was used in the overall asymmetry test (i.e., CGAM).
In the limb vs. joint kinematics test, limb kinematic parameters (LL,
LEA, FPA) and joint kinematic parameters (RoMs) were normalized
and then combined with the Mahalanobis distance, respectively, in
order to produce parameters from each limb and joint kinematic
domain into one value per session. For each side, we examined
how changes in each kinematic domain associated with changes
in functional gait recovery (i.e., gait speed).
2.5. Statistical analysis
R version 3.4.1 (2017 The R foundation for Statistical Comput-
ing) was used for the statistical analysis. For the analysis, 53 ses-
sions from a total of 56 recording sessions were used, excluding
outliers (8th session of P3, 9th session of P5, 2nd session of P6)
with an exaggerated range of motion (<60°) at ankle dorsi/plan-
tarflexion (e.g., distorted by magnetic interference of the IMUs).
A linear mixed regression model was used to evaluate the rela-
tionship between asymmetry of gait parameters and speed as a
functional gait measure with significance level of a < 0:05. For
the overall gait asymmetry test, the Mahalanobis distances of spa-
tiotemporal, limb and joint kinematics were standardized and used
as dependent variables. For the asymmetry test of individual
parameters, the asymmetry ratio, jarij, of each gait parameter
was used as a dependent variable. For both tests, gait speed and
subject were used as fixed and random effects of the mixed model,
respectively. In addition, a one-sided one-sample t-test was used to
evaluate the asymmetry of overall and individual gait parameters
at the maximum functional recovery with significance level of
a < 0:05. The asymmetry ratio at maximum gait speed of each
patient was extracted and compared with the symmetric threshold
value for each gait parameter from Table 2.
For the limb vs. joint kinematics test, the linear mixed regres-
sion model was used to evaluate the relations between parameters
of both kinematic domains and gait speed with significance level of
a < 0:05. Coefficient of determination (R2
) (Nakagawa and
Schielzeth, 2013), Akaike information criteria (AIC), and Bayesian
information criteria (BIC) were used to compare goodness-of-fit
of the models.
3. Results
3.1. Asymmetry of overall gait parameters
We first examined the relations of overall asymmetry over spa-
tiotemporal, limb and joint kinematic domains and gait speed over
the initial recovery phase of three months based on the CGAM.
Fig. 3 illustrates changes in the Mahalanobis distances of spa-
tiotemporal (left), limb (middle), and joint (right) kinematics
across changing gait speeds, respectively. The results indicated that
the asymmetry improved significantly in spatiotemporal (b = 0.
47, p<0.01) and limb kinematic parameters (b = 0.36, p<0.05)
whereas joint kinematics (b = 0.25, p = 0.14) revealed an improv-
ing trend. At the session with maximum functional recovery (max-
imum speed), spatiotemporal parameters (Dmax = 0.11, p=0.11) did
not reveal significant asymmetry but limb (Dmax = 0.56, p<0.001)
and joint (Dmax = 0.38, p<0.01) kinematic parameters remained sig-
nificantly different (asymmetric) compared to the symmetric
threshold. All results are summarized in Table 3.
3.2. Asymmetry of individual gait parameters
According to the overall asymmetry test, all gait parameters
revealed improving trends but both limb and joint kinematic
parameters remained asymmetric at the maximum functional
recovery. Thus, we used linear mixed regression models and one-
sided one-sample t-tests on individual gait parameters indepen-
dently to further investigate major contributors of overall gait
asymmetry. The results revealed that the asymmetry improved
significantly at SL (b = 0.33, p < 0.05), LEA (b = 0.65, p < 0.01),
and hip flex/extension (b = 0.15, p < 0.05). At maximum gait
speed, all limb kinematic parameters including LEA
(jarmaxj = 0.29, p < 0.05), LL (jarmaxj = 0.62, p < 0.01), and FPA
(jarmaxj = 0.87, p < 0.01) and joint kinematic parameters including

hip flex/extension (jarmaxj = 0.14, p < 0.05), hip abd/adduction
(jarmaxj = 0.29, p < 0.05), hip int/external rotation (jarmaxj = 0.36,
p < 0.01), and knee flex/extension (jarmaxj = 0.27, p < 0.05) remained
significantly different (i.e. asymmetric) compared to the symmetric
threshold (Table 4). As expected, both spatiotemporal parameters
(SL and ST) did not show significant differences from the symmet-
ric threshold.
3.3. Limb kinematics vs. joint kinematics
We examined whether limb kinematic parameters were prefer-
entially associated with functional gait recovery compared to joint
kinematics, consistent with the uncontrolled manifold hypothesis
(Chang et al., 2009). For each side, we transformed both limb and
joint kinematic parameters into a common space by combining
all parameters of each kinematic domain using the Mahalanobis
distance. A simple correlation analysis between limb and joint
kinematic domains revealed r = 0.67 and r = 0.38 for unaffected
and affected sides, respectively. The results revealed that all
kinematic parameters in all domains of both sides significantly
associated with gait speed (all p < 0.001). However, according to
the goodness-of-fit measures, the variance accounted for of limb
kinematic parameters (R2
= 41.9%) was greater than in joint kine-
matics (R2
= 33.1%) at the affected side, whereas unaffected side
showed a greater correlation in joint kinematics (R2
= 57.6%) than
limb kinematics (R2
= 27.5%) with consistent trends in AIC and BIC
(Table 5).
4. Discussion
Typical clinical outcomes focus more on gait function than qual-
ity (Hornby et al., 2016), resulting in very little knowledge of how
gait quality develops over the course of recovery. The primary goal
of this study was to establish initial evidence regarding measure-
ments of changes in gait quality over the early stage of recovery.
We observed that asymmetry of gait parameters overall improved
with gait function, but both limb and joint kinematics remained
asymmetric at the maximum functional recovery. Second, leg
extension and hip flex/extension were most associated with

regression model (Table 2).

--- PAGE 6 ---
improved asymmetry, but many gait parameters remained asym-
metric at the maximum functional recovery. Third, limb kinemat-
ics of the impaired side was preferentially associated with
functional gait recovery over joint kinematics. These results offer
preliminary evidence justifying the importance of gait quality in
stroke recovery and indicate a specific set of parameters that
may be more critical than others in the early recovery process.
Asymmetry in kinematics is often underreported in literature,
perhaps due to the difficulties in measuring kinematic data in clin-
ical settings. Based on our longitudinally measured gait kinematics
data from wearable IMUs, the spatiotemporal as well as kinematic
asymmetries were captured and evaluated along with the
improved gait speed over the course of early recovery. The results
of our overall asymmetry test indicated that all measures of asym-
metry improved with gait speed (Fig. 3). This result agrees with
earlier work that found faster and more symmetric walking
showed lower metabolic cost than merely walking faster or more
symmetrically (Awad et al., 2015).
We observed that leg extension angle and hip flex/extension
asymmetry measures were most associated with gait speed. This
suggests that the leg extension and hip flex/extension may be
important predictors of functional gait recovery. These results
agree with previous studies that found leg and hip extension were
significantly associated with propulsive forces during walking as
well as gait speed (Kim and Eng, 2004; Peterson et al., 2010). How-
ever, all parameters other than ankle dorsi/plantarflexion
remained significantly asymmetric compared to the healthy sym-
metric threshold at the maximum gait speed (Table 4). This could
mean that the underlying control system involved in gait recovery
prioritizes motion at the hip and leg extension over other gait
parameters. It may also suggest that there is still a room to
improve on those asymmetric gait parameters and additional ther-
apeutic efforts need to be made to achieve a complete recovery
with symmetric walking.
While all kinematic domains of both sides correlated with gait
speed, the results of goodness-of-fit measure revealed that the
variance explained by limb kinematic parameters (R2
= 41.9%)
was greater than joint kinematics (R2
= 33.1%) in the affected side,
indicating stronger association in limb kinematics with gait speed
over the joint kinematics on impaired side (see Table 5). The
goodness-of-fit measure for limb kinematics is similar to a clini-
cally relevant relationship between steps per session and recovery
(R2
= 42%) found by Hornby et al. (2016). We also observed an 8.8%
difference between goodness-of-fit measures of limb and joint
kinematics. While there is no basis of comparison to judge the
magnitude of this difference, the result itself suggests that post-
stroke individuals may preferentially coordinate limb function
using the limb kinematics and compensate in the joint kinematics.
These findings are consistent with the concept of an uncontrolled
manifold in joint kinematics space found previously in animal
models (Bauman and Chang, 2013; Chang et al., 2009).
In the unaffected side, joint kinematic parameters (R2
= 57.6%)
revealed greater explained variance than limb kinematics
(R2
= 27.5%). These results are contrary to the trends observed in
the affected limb and further, would seem contrary to the uncon-
trolled manifold hypothesis. While feasible that the uncontrolled
manifold hypothesis is not an ideal model, this finding may be
explained by greater residual function in the limb kinematics in
the unaffected limb compared to joint kinematics. Indeed, our
additional analysis revealed that the intercept of the unaffected
limb kinematics (0.39) was over two times greater than that of
the affected side (0.18) (Supplementary Fig. 1). This indicates that
a ceiling effect in the limb kinematics of the unaffected side may
reduce its explanatory ability. These results may provide insight
into how to interpret kinematic biomarkers of recovery.
This study represents a proof-of-concept to show how measures
of gait quality associate with changes in gait function in the most
critical stage of recovery. However, results need to be interpreted
with an important proviso. This study was limited to a small sam-
ple size of six patients with a restricted range of impairments (only
individuals who were able to walk within one month post-injury).
The study was also conducted at the same hospital with similar
training techniques. Thus, we cannot generalize these results to a
larger population of stroke patients. However, our data show the
feasibility of unobtrusively recording gait during therapy longitu-
dinally and offer a framework for how it can help improve our
understanding of recovery. We expect this study will justify more
expanded research on gait quality with a larger post-stroke popu-
lation for more reliable generalization.
Another important advance of this work is providing a novel
methodology to track gait quality by measuring joint kinematics
over the course of the initial recovery stage. However, measuring
joint kinematics is relatively more sensitive to errors than other
conventional gait measures such as gait speed or spatiotemporal
characteristics. Typical drawbacks of IMUs, magnetic distortion
(De Vries et al., 2009) and improper calibration in a straight stand-
ing posture, may have influenced our results. To mitigate this
issues, we used an IMU motion capture system specifically devel-
oped for measuring kinematics (Paulich et al., 2018) and validated
in a laboratory environment (Lee et al., 2019). Recalibration was
performed regularly by the experimenter based on visual inspec-
tion, although without any template to compare, it is possible
there were some errors in calibration. Given range-of-motion-
based outcome measures, it is unlikely that calibration issues sub-
stantially affected our results. We expect further advances in
motion capture technology will help to measure more accurate
kinematics data, providing more detailed and reliable results of
characterizing post-stroke gait.
5. Conclusions
The purpose of this observational study was to monitor changes
in gait quality with functional gait recovery longitudinally over the
initial recovery phase by unobtrusively measuring full lower body
kinematics. We observed that while post-stroke individuals

exhibited overall improvements in gait quality with gait function,
symmetry did not fully recover. We conclude that using inertial
motion capture to longitudinally observe gait quality is feasible
and may provide a more holistic representation of recovery. These
initial results justify further research on monitoring gait quality
with a larger clinical study.
